evidence: Cic. Off. 1.27: brevis est et ad tempus
Liv. 28.42.5: dux ad tempus lēctus (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: The classical way to say it: what is ad tempus lasts for a time, for the moment. The same words also mean “at the right time, on time” (ad tempus redīre, Cic. Att. 13.45.2, Lewis & Short; see on time); the context tells which.

terms.gloss: for the time being, for the occasion
evidence: Tac. Ann. 14.20: scaenā in tempus strūctā
Traupman 88–89: for the occasion, for the time being, in tempus
Sen. Ep. 9.9: amīcitiae, quās temporāriās populus appellat
terms.comment: Rare before Augustus (Nepos once); Seneca, the elder Pliny, Quintilian (Lewis & Short). It also means suited to the times, and so changeable: temporāria līberālitās (Nep. Att. 11), ingenia temporāria (Curt. 4.5.11).

terms.gloss: makeshift, put together in a hurry
terms.comment: Of what is got up in haste for an emergency: temporary shelters, stands, troops raised at short notice (subitāriī mīlitēs, Livy). Lewis & Short.

terms.gloss: Traupman’s “for the time being”; classically, as the occasion allows
evidence: Sall. Jug. 49.6: pauca prō tempore mīlitēs hortātus (Lewis & Short s.v. hortor)
terms.comment: In classical prose prō tempore is “to suit the occasion, as time allowed”; for “for the time being” in praesentiā (see now) and in tempus are clearer.

phrases.latin: perturbātiōne aliquā animī, quae plērumque brevis est et ad tempus
phrases.english: in some upset of the mind, which is mostly brief and temporary

phrases.latin: nam anteā subitāriīs gradibus et scaenā in tempus strūctā lūdōs ēdī solitōs
phrases.english: for (they said) games used to be given before on makeshift tiers, with a stage put up for the occasion

phrases.latin: Hae sunt amīcitiae, quās temporāriās populus appellat
phrases.english: These are the friendships that people call temporary
